Confirm with dermoscopy (looking for thrombosed capillaries) and/or punch biopsy ± HPV PCR if needed.

2) Punctate palmoplantar keratoderma (punctate PPK; mosaic or sporadic) — Fits punctate, keratotic lesions on palm that began in childhood; less likely without family history but mosaic/non‑familial forms occur. Confirm with punch biopsy (histology) and clinical review for additional lesions.

3) Epidermal nevus (localized/linear epidermal nevus or porokeratotic eccrine ostial and dermal duct nevus) — Early childhood onset, unilateral, localized distribution is typical; lesions can be hyperkeratotic and refractory to standard wart treatments. Diagnosis by clinical pattern and biopsy.

4) Punctate porokeratosis (porokeratosis punctata palmaris et plantaris) — Small punctate keratotic papules with a central keratin plug can appear on palms; usually shows cornoid lamella on histology. Consider if biopsy shows cornoid lamella.

5) Focal/acquired mechanical hyperkeratosis (callus or focal acral hyperkeratosis) — Less likely given very early onset and limited response to treatments, but still possible if long-standing repetitive pressure/trauma localized to that area.

Suggested next steps to confirm diagnosis (if you wish): noninvasive dermoscopic exam of the papules and a 2–3 mm punch biopsy for histopathology (and HPV PCR if wart is suspected).
